name: OpenMP parallel all-pairs nearest-neighbor distance (The C++ Programmer's Mindset, ch. 4)
baseline: sequential nested-loop version of the same all-pairs minimum-distance computation (nearest_neighbor_distance_seq, one thread)
workload: All-pairs minimum Euclidean distance (std::hypot on float Point2D) over 65,536 random points in [-1,1]^2, an O(n^2) triangular double loop, timed per call with Google Benchmark in milliseconds; the OpenMP version adds '#pragma omp parallel for reduction(min:...)' on the outer loop.
claimed_speedup: About 4x faster with 8 threads: 4,797 ms sequential versus 1,161 ms with OpenMP (ratio 4.1x derived from those two figures; book figures as paraphrased in the seed lead, not on the repo page).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Chapter-04/CMakeLists.txt requires C++20, OpenMP and Google Benchmark and sets no build type or optimisation flags, so the optimisation level depends on how the reader configures CMake.
hardware: Not stated (book: 8 threads; CPU model not given in the lead).
stars_or_usage: 20 stars (Packt companion repository for the 2025 book)
tradeoffs: Needs an OpenMP runtime and compiler support. The outer loop is triangular (iteration i does n-i-1 inner steps), so the default static schedule leaves the threads with unequal work (code reading); 4.1x on 8 threads is about 52% parallel efficiency. The O(n^2) algorithm is unchanged; a spatial index (k-d tree or grid) would change the complexity, which this record does not claim.
caveats: The numbers are the book's own figures as paraphrased in the seed lead; they are not printed anywhere on the repository pages opened (the repo holds the benchmark code and no results), and the book itself was deliberately not consulted. Baseline is the book's own single-threaded loop, so this shows OpenMP scaling on a toy kernel, not an improvement on a library or std facility (nearest_neighbor.cpp includes <execution> but does not use parallel algorithms). Compiler, flags and CPU are not stated, so no tier A. Input points are re-randomised each run from std::random_device. Tier C: first-party book measurement.

name: Cache-blocked double-precision matrix multiply with tile accumulator (The C++ Programmer's Mindset, ch. 4)
baseline: naive i-j-k triple-loop dgemm (dgemm_basic in the same repo, no blocking); OpenBLAS cblas_dgemm is measured as a reference and is far faster than the blocked code
workload: Dense square row-major double matrix multiply (alpha=1, beta=0), time per multiplication with Google Benchmark in ms; the repo's bench_gemm.cpp uses 1000x1000 matrices (the book shows the size only in an image); blocked variant uses block size 32 with a local tile accumulator.
claimed_speedup: Basic 547 ms, blocked (block size 32) 289 ms, OpenBLAS 24.1 ms per multiplication; blocked is about 1.9x faster than basic (derived), OpenBLAS about 12x faster than blocked and 23x faster than basic (derived); book figures as paraphrased in the seed lead, not on the repo page. Averages over 39 (basic), 73 (blocked) and 874 (OpenBLAS) iterations.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Chapter-04/CMakeLists.txt adds '-g -pg -fno-omit-frame-pointer' to the bench_gemm target and sets no optimisation level; BLAS comes from CMake FindBLAS (static, 8-byte integers requested, cblas.h from /usr/include/openblas).
stars_or_usage: 20 stars (Packt companion repository for the 2025 book)
tradeoffs: Teaching-level blocking only: scalar inner loops, no packing, no SIMD, no threading. It is not a replacement for OpenBLAS, MKL, BLIS or Eigen, which are an order of magnitude faster in the book's own numbers.
caveats: The numbers are the book's own figures as paraphrased in the seed lead; they are not printed anywhere on the repository pages opened (the repo holds the benchmark code and no results), and the book itself was deliberately not consulted. The only baseline beaten is the book's own naive loop; against the real incumbent (OpenBLAS) the technique is about 12x slower. The benchmark target is built with -pg (gprof mcount on every non-inlined function entry) and -fno-omit-frame-pointer; the effect on the inner loops depends on inlining and optimisation level, neither of which is stated. Matrix 'a' is default-constructed (uninitialised) in the benchmark. dgemm_blocked contains assert(a.is_row_major()) with lowercase names that do not exist, so the file only compiles with assertions disabled (NDEBUG), i.e. a Release-type build. Compiler and CPU not stated. Tier C: first-party book measurement.

name: SAXPY function multiversioning with per-ISA builds and CPUID dispatch (The C++ Programmer's Mindset, ch. 4)
baseline: default-target build of the same scalar saxpy loop (saxpy_default, x86-64 SSE2 baseline, no runtime dispatch); OpenBLAS cblas_saxpy measured as a reference
workload: y[i] += a*x[i] over 5,120 floats (N = 5*1024), Google Benchmark time per call in ns, comparing the same loop compiled for default, -msse4.2, -mavx2 and -mavx512f, a hand-written AVX2 intrinsics version, and cblas_saxpy; ct::saxpy picks the best one via CPUID.
claimed_speedup: Vector size 5120: default 329 ns, sse4.2 330 ns, hand-crafted AVX2 298 ns, avx2 259 ns, avx512f 243 ns; OpenBLAS saxpy 278 ns. avx512f build about 1.35x and avx2 build about 1.27x faster than the default build (derived); both slightly ahead of OpenBLAS (278/243 about 1.14x, 278/259 about 1.07x, derived). Book figures as paraphrased in the seed lead, not on the repo page.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; the lead implies GCC -O3. Chapter-04/CMakeLists.txt compiles saxpy.cpp.in once per ISA via configure_file with per-source -msse4.2 / -mavx2 / -mavx512f (or /arch: on MSVC) and saxpy_hand.cpp with -mavx2; no build type is set. The repo does NOT use [[gnu::target_clones]] for this chapter-4 benchmark (Chapter-14/saxpy_mt.cpp does use target_clones("avx2,default") for its CPU saxpy).
hardware: Not stated (an AVX-512 capable CPU is implied by the avx512f row).
stars_or_usage: 20 stars (Packt companion repository for the 2025 book)
tradeoffs: Several copies of the same loop plus a runtime CPUID dispatcher (my_cpuid.h, get_best_instructions.h); larger binary and an indirect dispatch per call, which dominates at small sizes. x86-only intrinsics and CPUID code. The SSE4.2 build matches the default build (330 versus 329 ns), probably because SSE2 already vectorises the loop.
caveats: The numbers are the book's own figures as paraphrased in the seed lead; they are not printed anywhere on the repository pages opened (the repo holds the benchmark code and no results), and the book itself was deliberately not consulted. Single small size (20 KB per vector, cache resident); the book itself warns that OpenBLAS call overhead may distort this size. The gains (1.1-1.35x) come from compiler auto-vectorisation at a wider ISA, not from a new algorithm; the 'default' baseline is deliberately the lowest ISA tier. The benchmark main() uses switch fall-through so a given CPU registers every lower tier too. CPU model, compiler and flags not stated. Tier C: first-party book measurement.

name: Clamp loop with conditional store instead of std::min (The C++ Programmer's Mindset, ch. 4)
baseline: std::min-based clamp loop (ct::clamp_min, branch-free/cmov form), same function with auto-vectorisation disabled on both sides
workload: Clamp 1,000 uint16_t values to a maximum of 0xFF (255) in place; values drawn uniformly from 0..65535 and regenerated outside the timed region each iteration (PauseTiming/ResumeTiming); Google Benchmark time per call.
claimed_speedup: Average 605 ns for the std::min (cmov) version versus 500 ns for the conditional-store version, about 1.2x faster (derived from those figures); book figures as paraphrased in the seed lead, not on the repo page. The book calls the improvement modest.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; the lead says GCC assembly is shown. clamp_loop.cpp marks both functions [[gnu::optimize("no-tree-vectorize")]]; CMakeLists.txt sets no build type or optimisation flags.
stars_or_usage: 20 stars (Packt companion repository for the 2025 book)
tradeoffs: Micro-idiom, not a library: whether a branch beats cmov depends on how predictable the data are, so the result flips on other distributions.
caveats: The numbers are the book's own figures as paraphrased in the seed lead; they are not printed anywhere on the repository pages opened (the repo holds the benchmark code and no results), and the book itself was deliberately not consulted. With a threshold of 0xFF and uniform uint16_t input, about 99.6% of elements exceed the threshold (derived from the repo constants), so the branch is almost always taken and well predicted: the favourable case for the branchy version. Vectorisation is switched off for both functions, which hides the SIMD min a normal -O3 build would use for std::min and makes the comparison unrepresentative of production builds. CPU, compiler version and flags not stated. Tier C: first-party book measurement.

name: Hash maps versus ordered maps, random-access lookup (The C++ Programmer's Mindset, ch. 5, Table 5.1)
workload: Random-key lookup via operator[] on a map holding int64 keys 0..n-1 (n = 256 and 1024), Google Benchmark CPU ns per lookup, including the per-iteration std::mt19937_64 draw; eight maps compared: std::map, std::unordered_map, absl::btree_map, absl::flat_hash_map, absl::node_hash_map, boost::container::flat_map, boost::unordered_map, boost::unordered_flat_map.
claimed_speedup: Hash maps roughly 10x faster than ordered maps, lookup time nearly flat with size. CPU ns at 256/1024 keys: std::map 23.3/34.9, std::unordered_map 3.56/3.81, absl::btree_map 19.5/24.1, absl::flat_hash_map 3.81/3.89, absl::node_hash_map 3.95/4.29, boost::container::flat_map 25.9/31.4, boost::unordered_map 3.68/3.66, boost::unordered_flat_map 3.93/4.03 (std::unordered_map is about 6.5x and 9.2x faster than std::map, derived). Book figures as paraphrased in the seed lead, not on the repo page.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Chapter-05/CMakeLists.txt sets C++20, no build type or optimisation flags; vcpkg.json pins abseil >= 20240722.0 and boost-container/-container-hash/-unordered >= 1.86.0.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7900x (per the book as paraphrased in the lead; not recorded in the repo).
stars_or_usage: 20 stars (Packt companion repository for the 2025 book)
tradeoffs: Hash maps give no ordered iteration or range queries and need a hash function; std::unordered_map is node-based with stable references, absl/boost flat variants are not reference-stable. The comparison says ordered versus hashed, not which hash map is best.
caveats: The numbers are the book's own figures as paraphrased in the seed lead; they are not printed anywhere on the repository pages opened (the repo holds the benchmark code and no results), and the book itself was deliberately not consulted. The data show absl::flat_hash_map and boost::unordered_flat_map are NOT faster than std::unordered_map at these sizes (3.81-4.03 ns versus 3.56-3.81 ns), so the win is hashing versus tree, not the third-party libraries; the book says flat and node variants did not differ because the data fit in cache. Only two tiny, cache-resident sizes; keys are inserted in ascending order, and the timed region includes the random-number generation (a few ns), which compresses the ratios. Standard library (libstdc++/libc++) and compiler flags not stated. Tier C: first-party book measurement with the CPU stated but not the flags.

name: Static CRTP dispatch versus virtual calls (Eli Bendersky benchmark)
baseline: virtual function call through a base-class pointer (run_dynamic version of the same loop)
workload: Synthetic O(N^2) loop that calls a trivial 'tick' method on objects, once through a virtual call on a base pointer and once through CRTP static dispatch; wall-clock run time of the whole loop.
claimed_speedup: run_dynamic 1.25 s versus run_crtp 0.21 s on an Intel i7-4771, about 6x faster (derived); the author reportedly expected about 2x. Snippet only: figures come from web-search result summaries of the post, which also cite a Hacker News comment quoting 1.25 s for the dynamic version (about 8e8 virtual calls, 1.5 ns per call).
stars_or_usage: Widely cited blog post (2013-12-05); also cited by the book as the source for the dispatch-cost gap
tradeoffs: CRTP binds the call at compile time so the compiler can inline it, but gives no runtime polymorphism: no heterogeneous containers of base pointers, no plug-ins, one template instantiation per type (code size, compile time). Virtual dispatch keeps a vptr per object and an indirect call.
caveats: Snippet only: eli.thegreenplace.net is blocked from this environment (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so the page was never opened; the numbers and CPU come from WebSearch result summaries (two searches agreeing on 1.25 s for the dynamic run, one giving 0.21 s for CRTP), and compiler and flags were not seen (null). The code is inline in the article; the eliben/code-for-blog 2013 directory has no matching file, so no repo carries it and no license was seen (usability reference). One trivial method in a tight loop: the large gap is mostly inlining (a secondary source says so), the worst case for virtual calls; a real gap depends on method size and cache behaviour. 2013-era CPU and compiler. Tier C: single first-party blog measurement, methodology not verified.
